notes.note: Weigall, citing Plutarch, describes Antony's relationship with his soldiers: their devotion to him, and his care for the wounded after battle. This bears on the morale and loyalty of the forces he led.
notes.quotation: He was adored by his soldiers, who, it is said, preferred his good opinion of them to their very lives.

notes.note: Weigall reads Antony's loss of Actium as the result of a sudden impulse on his part, one instance of his impatient character; he does not say what the impulse was in this passage.
notes.quotation: The battle of Actium, which ended his career, was lost by a sudden impulse on his part

notes.note: Weigall's own inference that Antony wanted the alliance with Cleopatra for a numerical (military) advantage over Octavian. It is the author's reconstruction of motive. It is set before Actium and states no force, command or operation.
notes.quotation: he saw in the alliance with Cleopatra the means whereby he could obtain a numerical advantage over his rival

notes.note: Weigall's hedged reading of Antony's plans: an alliance with Cleopatra would put her money, men and ships at his disposal. This is military resourcing seen through his own inference, before the Actium campaign.
notes.quotation: firstly, the formation of an offensive and defensive alliance with Cleopatra, in order that her money, men, and ships might be placed at his disposal

notes.note: Weigall's own hedged reasoning that Antony, having given 130 ships to Octavian in 37 BCE, would look to Cleopatra's large Egyptian navy to make up the loss. It bears on the origin of the eastern fleet later seen at Actium, but the passage does not link it to that battle.

notes.note: Weigall's hedged reconstruction of Cleopatra's advice that Antony drop the Parthian war and turn on Octavian and Rome. It is his own speculation, not a recorded speech, and it is preparatory to the Actium war.
